title: Philadelphia (Revelation 3:7–13)
hook: little strength, but an open door no one can shut

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sardis: a church with a name for being alive, told to wake up and strengthen what remains. Your line was wake up. What did you do once with your full attention? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five.

"Thou hast a little strength." An odd line to find in a letter of praise. Not great strength. Not hidden reserves. A little. That's what the risen Christ says to the church in Philadelphia, and he doesn't say it as a scolding. In the same breath he tells them that a door has been set open in front of them, and nobody can shut it. A small church, low on strength, standing in front of a door it didn't open and can't be locked out of. That's today's word. And since it's the end of the week, we'll stand back at the end and look at all the letters so far.

First, who's speaking: "he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth." That's an echo of Isaiah, where a steward is handed the key of the house of David: "so he shall open, and none shall shut." The key isn't the church's. That's the point. Second, the door itself: "behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name." Listen to the order. The door isn't a prize for being strong. It's set open for people with a little strength who kept going. What the door is, readers differ. Some hear a door for sharing the gospel, the way Paul writes that "a great door and effectual is opened unto me." Others hear the door into God's kingdom. The letter doesn't stop to say. Third, a promise for people who feel small: "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out." A pillar holds a building up and never gets moved out. Fourth, the week. It opened on Patmos with fear not. Ephesus was asked to return to its first love. Smyrna, poor but rich, was promised a crown of life. Pergamum got a white stone and a new name. Thyatira grew, more than at first. Sardis was told to wake up. And Philadelphia, with its little strength, got a door. In the King James text, each letter turns to its church with the same words: I know thy works. These letters are written to churches that someone is paying attention to.
screen: `A PILLAR THAT GOES NO MORE OUT.`
`A WEEK OF LETTERS: I KNOW THY WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk through an open door. If you can, stand and go to the nearest doorway. Pause on the threshold. Notice the frame, the air on each side. Then step through slowly, and stay there a moment. If you can't move right now, picture a door you go through every day, and walk through it in your mind. Then settle, and breathe, and ask: what door is already open in my life that I've been waiting to feel strong enough for? If you pray, you can name it to God. If you don't, just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Philadelphia. The church with a little strength, which kept the word, and was set before an open door that no one can shut.

Your line: an open door. Today, walk through one door that's already open for you, an invitation, a chance, a conversation, without waiting to feel stronger first. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Christians sometimes speak of an 'open door' when a new chance to serve or to share their faith appears, borrowing the language of Revelation 3:8 and of Paul's letters.

notes: Week-end look-back names the days 1289–1294 (Patmos, Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis) by their carries; confirm against the written scripts for 1289–1291.

'In the King James text, each letter opens the same way: I know thy works.' True of the KJV (Revelation 2:2, 9, 13, 19; 3:1, 8, 15); some Greek texts lack 'works' in 2:9 and 2:13. Confirm the hedge is enough.
The meaning of the open door is given two ways (mission, cf. 1 Corinthians 16:9; entry to the kingdom), unranked. Confirm.
The city's name is not glossed (no etymology given) by design.
